opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the big lesson of the last several years is that generality wins. When you train one very large model on a huge amount of data, it picks up an enormous amount about the world, including medicine. It's read the textbooks, the papers, the case discussions, the forum posts where people describe their symptoms. A lot of the knowledge a doctor needs is already in there.

And medicine isn't really a narrow task. A good doctor has to understand what the patient is saying, often vaguely or emotionally. They have to reason under uncertainty, weigh tradeoffs, explain things clearly, and know when to say "I don't know, go see a specialist." Those are general intelligence skills: language, reasoning, communication, common sense. If you build a small specialized model, you'd have to rebuild all of that from scratch, and you'd probably do it worse.

So economically, it makes more sense to put your effort into making the general model smarter. Every improvement there lifts medicine, law, coding, education, and companionship all at once. Then you add a bit on top: some fine-tuning, the right prompting, access to a patient's records, maybe retrieval over current clinical guidelines, and a lot of care around safety and evaluation. But the core intelligence is shared.

Historically, people built special-purpose systems for each domain. Then a general model came along and just beat all of them. I expect the same thing here. The AI doctor will be the general model, with a little bit of domain-specific scaffolding, not a separate brain.

r001.rationale: The response says improving a general model makes more economic sense, but does not state that general-purpose LLMs are inexpensive relative to human doctors or that this price comparison rules out a task-specific model.

r002.rationale: It does not claim price is the only reason to use task-specific models.

r003.rationale: It says large models learn from huge amounts of data, but does not suggest that analyzing data with low marginal value justifies a targeted model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the reason is that the general-purpose model is going to be better at it. If you look at what it takes to be a good doctor, it's not just knowing medicine. It's understanding the patient, understanding language, understanding the context of their life, reasoning about ambiguous information, knowing when to ask a follow-up question. That's basically everything. The skills that make a model good at medicine are the same skills that make it good at everything else, and you get those from training on all of human knowledge, not from a narrow slice of it.

And the economics push the same direction. The big general model is where all the compute and all the effort goes. If you take some tiny fraction of that budget and train a medical-only model, you end up with something that's worse on the general stuff and probably not even better on the medical stuff, because the medical knowledge was already in the big model. Most of what a specialized system needs can be handled by giving the general model the right context, the right tools, maybe some fine-tuning or a system prompt that says "you're a doctor, be careful, here's the patient's history." That's cheap. Training a separate frontier-quality model is not.

There's also just a practical point about where the value actually is. The hard part of a high-value application like this usually isn't the model's intelligence, it's everything around it. Regulation, trust, liability, integrating with the hospital, getting the data in. The model is the easy part, in some sense, and it keeps getting better on its own every time the big labs release a new one. If you've bet on a task-specific model, you have to keep retraining it to stay competitive. If you've bet on the general model, you just upgrade.

So I'd say the only places you really want specialized models are where there's some constraint the general model can't meet, like it has to run on a device, or it has to be extremely cheap at enormous scale. A doctor doesn't need to be cheap in that sense. A doctor needs to be smart. And smart is what the general model gives you.

r001.rationale: The response says a separate frontier model is expensive to train and that doctors need intelligence, but it does not say general-purpose models are already inexpensive relative to human doctors.

r002.rationale: It gives device constraints as another reason to use a specialized model, so it does not claim price is the only reason.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that analyzing large quantities of low-marginal-value data could justify a targeted model.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of what you want from an AI doctor is the same thing you want from any really good model: it needs to know a lot, reason well, and understand what you're telling it. Medicine isn't an isolated task. You're dealing with language, biology, people's behavior, and incomplete information. So having broad capabilities is very useful.

You might still give it medical instructions, access to relevant information, and tools. And you'd certainly want to test it very carefully. But that doesn't necessarily mean you need a separate model. If the general model can understand the problem and apply the relevant knowledge, then being a doctor becomes an application of that intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says a separate model may not be needed because broad capabilities can handle medicine, but it does not mention the cost of general models relative to human doctors.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that price is the only reason to use task-specific models.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that analyzing vast quantities of data with low marginal value could justify a targeted model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of what makes a good doctor is just being smart and knowing a lot of things. And those are the same things we’re trying to get into the general model. Medicine isn’t this completely isolated domain—you need to reason, communicate with people, understand what they’re telling you, and bring together information from different places.

So I’d expect the best general model, with access to the right medical information and tools, to be a very good starting point. You’d still need to test it very carefully and build the application around it. But the fact that the application is really valuable doesn’t necessarily mean you need to train a separate brain for it.
